vignette:
Shivani is a 32-year-old school counselor, married and living in a quiet Midwestern suburb, but the life she occupies now feels like a stage set that could collapse at any moment. The event that dismantled her sense of safety happened three years ago, during a visit to her extended family in a region that had, until then, been merely a place of childhood summers. A sudden escalation of local conflict trapped her and several family members in a marketplace for nearly six hours. Gunfire and explosions came from multiple directions, and people around her were injured. She remembers the precise, terrible weight of pressing herself flat behind a concrete barrier, her younger cousin’s hand clamped in hers, the sound of a child screaming somewhere she could not see. She remembers thinking, with a clarity that still visits her in nightmares, that she was supposed to get them out. She was the one from America, the one who was supposed to know what to do. And she did nothing. She held a child’s hand and hid.

In the months that followed her return to the United States, Shivani did not speak about the marketplace. She told her husband she was tired, that the jet lag had been worse than expected, that she needed to focus on the new school year. But the feeling that she had failed did not fade. It calcified into a conviction she carried silently: she should have protected the others, and she had not. This thought did not arrive as a memory she chose to examine; it was simply the background hum of her mind, the truth beneath every ordinary moment. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like fact, that she was a weak person. The person who had once organized crisis drills at her school, who had calmly mediated between distraught parents and anxious administrators, who had prided herself on being steady in a storm—that person, she was certain, had been a performance. The real Shivani, the one who had lain on a dirty floor and prayed, was someone else entirely. She was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined her. She felt this as a physical contraction in her chest when she walked into her office each morning.

The consequences of this belief reshaped her life slowly and thoroughly. At work, she began to avoid the hallway near the main entrance during dismissal, where the noise and crowding triggered a visceral sense of being trapped. She stopped volunteering to supervise field trips or community events. Her principal noticed and asked if she was unwell; she smiled and said she was fine, just stretched thin. At home, she stopped taking the bus or the subway, even for short errands. Public transport had become unbearable—the press of bodies, the inability to see an exit, the sudden stops that made her heart pound so hard she thought she might faint. She began driving everywhere, even to the grocery store three blocks away, and found herself scanning parking lots for escape routes before she got out of the car.

The most deliberate strategy she adopted was her clothing. Shivani started wearing loose, dark, concealing garments—oversized jackets, hooded sweaters, scarves that could be pulled up. She told her husband it was a new style preference, but privately she was certain that being noticed was dangerous. If no one saw her, if she made herself small and forgettable, she could not be targeted. She began to believe that visibility itself was a kind of vulnerability. Her husband grew confused and then concerned; he asked if she was depressed, if she wanted to talk to someone. She deflected. She did not know how to explain that the danger she felt was not in her head but in the world, that she was simply seeing it clearly now.

What finally brought Shivani to seek help was not a dramatic crisis but a quiet erosion. A student came to her office in tears, describing a panic attack after a lockdown drill at school. Shivani sat across from her, offered tissues, breathed slowly, and felt nothing. She felt hollow. She realized, with a cold shock, that she could no longer access the compassion that had once been her most natural resource. She was going through the motions of her job, but she was not present. She was afraid, and she was tired, and she could not remember the last time she had felt capable of anything at all. When she called to schedule her first appointment, she told the intake coordinator she wanted help with anxiety. She did not say that she was most afraid of discovering that her weakness was not a symptom but a truth—that the person she used to be was gone, and that no amount of therapy could bring her back. But she came anyway, and that, she thought bitterly, might be the only proof she had left that she was still fighting.
